Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Fairbairn
This, being our last newsletter of 2021, has me
looking back at the Guild’s activities over the past
year. While there have been, and continue to be,
challenges related to the pandemic, we’ve had
many successes.
Our website was awarded the AAW’s top club
website of the year. Our membership grew a bit
and we welcomed new members from other
provinces and states. We’ve been so fortunate to
have been able to provide a record number of interactive remote demonstrations (IRDs) from so
many world class turners. Participation in our
monthly online Tech Talks has never been better.
Likewise, our weekly online Dessert Chats are always a fun diversion that help keep us all connected regardless of where we are.
Our recent wood raffle of 140+ boxes of wood
donated by Barry Wilkinson was a big success for
both the GVWG and our neighbouring Fraser Valley Woodturners Guild. All proceeds from the
raffle were divided between the two clubs based
on the wishes of each ticket purchaser.
During our last monthly meeting in October, I presented Barry Wilkinson with the GVWG Outstanding Contribution Award. This award, of course,
was in the works for weeks prior to Barry’s generous donation of his huge stash of turning wood.
This past weekend a few of us were able to meet
in person with Barry to present him with his
award. See elsewhere in the newsletter for a
photo and details about the award.
For those members who have been procrastinating, please make sure you renew your memberships and submit your dues as soon as possible
as we will soon be updating our email lists and
you may stop receiving links to our meetings.
As always, stay safe and keep turning!
Steve

Editor’s NotesBy Steve Fairbairn
This month’s Guild Member Profile features Bob
James, a long time member, current board member and past Treasurer of the GVWG.
Sheila Balzer returns this month with her monthly
column chronicling her journey as a new turner.
This month Sheila describes the excitement of being able to receive some in-person, hands-on training that has been unavailable to her since the beginning of the pandemic when she first started
turning.
Ed Pretty describes his experience turning a couple
species of wood that he, in his decades of experience, had not turned before.
As usual, I’m always on the hunt for articles from
our semi-regular and new contributors and any
turning related topic they care to pontificate
about. Please consider writing any length of article
telling us about your latest projects, tips & tricks,
techniques you’ve either mastered or are in the
process of learning, or even just your philosophy
on woodturning. All submissions can be emailed to
editor@gvwg.ca.
Steve

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
Tech TalkBy Bruce Campbell
Tech Talk is held on the Monday evening following
the Guild ZOOM session. The credentials for the
session are sent to all registered Guild members
and all are encouraged to participate in the freeflowing discussion centered on technical aspects of
woodturning.
The Tech Talk Zoom session was well attended this
month as usual. Thanks you all, in advance, for
your contributions, be they questions, comments,
or suggestions.
Filling In the Gap
Dan started us off with an annoying problem and a
solution. There is a “gap” between the smallest
tenon that #3 jaws will clamp down on and the
largest one that #2 jaws can expand to grip. This
can be VERY annoying if you just changed jaws and
they still don’t fit.
Dan’s simple solution is to remove two opposite
jaws from the larger set. This allows more room
for the remaining jaws to close on the tenon. It will
still have reasonable grip with the four corners of
the remaining jaws biting in the wood. But, this is
just a quick fix to get out of a difficult situation rather than a regular way to grip a work piece.
Exploding Reeves Drive Pulley
Terry shared a sad story of having one side of an
aluminum Reeves pulley shatter. She was concerned that she had done something wrong but,
after some discussion we felt it was likely a flaw in
the pulley.
I did recommend that folks with Reeves drives
make sure to keep the sliding shafts well lubricated
and Larry suggested that belts can sometimes look
fine but have worn until they are too thin to work
properly.
Alas, this seems to be a common problem with the
older vintage of lathes because replacements for
that system are no longer available. The good
thing is that now Terry has a great excuse to get e
new lathe.
Convenient Roll-Away Photo Backdrop
Theo sent in his solution for a photo backdrop in
his shop. He writes:
(Continued on page 5)

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
“I was playing in the shop this weekend trying to
devise a better photography studio without major
setup time. I installed a shelf/valance above my
drawing table; inserted a white roller shade (Home
Depot), and changed the overhead light to one
from Costco as suggested a previous Tech Talk. It
seems to work well without all the fuss. The bonus
is I have a resting spot for the "magic wand" .”
Nice simple solution, Theo. Now if I could just find
a flat spot in my shop that is not covered in “stuff”.
UV Glue – A New Way to Connect
UV gluing systems are getting more attention these
days most likely because of frequent TV ads. This
works by applying a small amount using a glue
dropper (much like CA glue) and then shining a UV
light on it for a few seconds. The light activates the
glue and it sets completely.
There are two variants of this system that are readily available at hardware stores and on-line; hard
and flexible. The glue is sold in black plastic bottles
or as a kit that includes a
UV flashlight.
An important thing to remember with this product
is that it must be exposed
to UV light to set. Therefore, it is not effective for
gluing wooden surfaces
together. But, for attaching anything transparent
like glass beads or clear
plastic it is great. I think
that we will see more and
more inventive uses of UV
glues just as we have done
with CA glues.
Blushing Lacquer
Gary reported that he had tried spraying rattle-can
lacquer in his usual warm location but got a milky
blush. He had just purchased a new batch with
more solids than his previous batch and it was raining heavily at the time. Larry suggested that the
combination of the additional solids and the humidity was the culprit. A suggestion was that he
respray when it gets drier and the new layer would
melt the previous one and clear the blush. Gary
elected to return to his previous mixture since it
seems to be humid in our area a lot of the time.
Obliterating Wood Grain Under Paint
Michael asked how to obliterate any sign of wood
grain in painted wood. After the gasps of “Why
would you do that?” dies down several suggestions
were put forward. One was to mix plaster of Paris
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)
Retracted
Extended

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
with lacquer sanding sealer. This fills the pores of
the wood and levels out the surface.
This lead to us revisit several excellent books on
wood finishing. They include:
•
Understanding Wood Finishes – Bob Flexner
•
The Wood Finishing Book – Michael Dresdner
•
Adventures in Wood Finishing – George Frank.
Electric Chainsaw Review – Oregon 1500CS
Phil reports that his newly purchased Oregon
1500CS with an 18” bar has made it much easier to
cut wood in his quiet neighbourhood. In addition,
he reports that it has plenty of power and cuts
beautifully. It has an on-board sharpener but several people suggested it was not good to use since
it sharpens the tops of the teeth and eventually
wears them down to the height of the rackers
which ruins the cut.
Diana added that she is really pleased with her
Dewalt 16” 20V battery-powered unit and while
electric saws cannot replace the independence and
power of a gas unit they are excellent alternatives
for at-home wood hacking.
Novel Vessel Steady Rest
Larry proposed a novel suggestion for a steady rest
system when doing hollow forms. He purchased
two ONEWAY bowl steady rests and placed one in
the usual location (see image below) and the other
on the opposite side or the piece. When set up in
that way the vessel is supported by four wheels
and really helps to dampen the vibrations that
plague everyone when making hollow forms.
Thanks, Larry.
Laguna Revo Banjo Clamp
Fraser remembered a previous report of a member
breaking the toolrest clamp on his Laguna lathe
and wanted to know how to prevent it. I have one
of these lathes and my solution was to insert a
washer in the slot. This allows me to clamp the
toolrest enough that it does not slip but prevents
the overtightening that causes the banjo to break.
3D-printed Magnetic Light Strip
Daniel has been working with 3D modeling and
used it to design a carrier to hold a short strip of
LED lights and 3 small magnets. After printing out
the holder with his 3D printer he wired it to a basic
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
power supply and now has a light that he can
attach to his banjo to light the interior of bowls.
Steve made a similar light by gluing magnets and
an LED strip to an old Meccano strip. He also wired
his to a basic power supply.
Not being good with any of the skills these two
showed, I bought a similar unit from our good
friend Cindy Drozda. Any way you choose to go,
there is no longer any excuse for not having
enough light to see what you are doing inside a
piece.
Index Indicator for Older Oneway
Steve F. purchased a
wonderful old ONEWAY
2436 with an index system that is cumbersome to use. However,
Oneway published a
“fix” for the problem
that involves masking
tape across the opening
on the top of the headstock. Steve took the
time
to
implement
different fix. It involves
making an indicator bar that is laid across the
headstock pulleys with a marker on it to align each
index point and held in place with rare earth magnets.
ONEWAY has since redesigned the indexer to make
this unnecessary but it is a good idea for other
lathes that may have the same challenge.
As usual, the session lasted nearly 2 hours with lots
of ideas, suggestions and laughs. Thanks to all for
you that participated. Please plan to join us next
time – 7:00PM Monday November 29th, 2021 via
(Continued from page 6)
7pm on the Monday after each monthly guild meeting
Bring your problems - Show off a new tool or invention - Share
your knowledge
Watch your email for the Zoom link!

Barry Wilkinson Presented with the GVWG Outstanding Contribution AwardBy Steve Fairbairn
There are people within any group that, by their
actions, leadership, guidance, or hard work, significantly define the group. They are the ones without
whom the group would undoubtedly be different.
They are the ones whose contributions shape the
group, give it direction, purpose, and richness. The
GVWG Outstanding Contribution Award is intended
to honour those people.
During the October online meeting, I was honoured
to be able to present Barry Wilkinson with the
GVWG Outstanding Contribution Award in recognition and appreciation for his many years of exceptional and outstanding contributions including
Newsletter Publisher, Treasurer, Turning 101 Coordinator and Board Member for the GVWG.
This past weekend Barry was presented with his
award plaque, crafted by Ed Pretty, and his framed
award certificate at his home.
Barry also becomes a lifetime member of the
Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild.
From the left: Steve Hansen (VP), Barry Wilkinson, Steve Fairbairn (President), Ed Pretty

Wood ReportBy Ed Pretty
Back in my schooling days, both high school and
post-secondary, we had to write book reports.
Partly to prove we read the book (Once in high
school I did mine from the inside jacket review the
night before. Got 10 out of 10), but also to outline
what we understood or learned from the book. In
that last regard, I thought I would do a “Wood Report” on a couple of woods that I turned recently
but had never presented an edge to before.
Weeping Willow:
You say, “You must have been desperate to turn
weeping willow”. I was. I was requested to provide
several sculptural forms for a collaboration – with a
deadline. I needed fresh, green wood but the stars
didn’t align to provide any out of the blue and my
usual sources were coming up empty. A notice
came to the guild through the “info@” email that a
Weeping Willow was available in Ioco. Truly, in desperation, I jumped on it.
It had very white sapwood with darker heart wood.
I used the stems (first branches from the trunk) for
what I needed to turn which had some interesting
clusters of buds all over. These clusters yielded
some very attractive “paisley” patterns in the outer
sapwood. They weren’t deep so it would have been
easy to turn them away. I turned the heartwood
completely away on these forms (these pieces
were turned end-grain), but I would think the contrast would have been attractive (I couldn’t have
contrasting wood in these forms anyway). For
these collaborations, I normally choose absolutely
plain, straight grain wood so as not to fight with
the native designs painted on them. The paisley
designs were attractive enough and spaced out
enough that the artist who requested these immediately decided to work them into his designs. He’s
very contemporary as First Nation artists go, so he
welcomed this first-time diversion.
As suspected, the wood was fairly soft. Not so soft
as to be delicate, but it was fairly easily marked.
The most undesirable trait of the wood was that it
was very “stringy” to rip with the chainsaw and
turn. It clogged the chain and gouge quite a bit,
mostly in the outer sapwood and cambium. I had
to work the pieces once they dried; carving and
sanding was not difficult. The wood didn’t seem to
be abrasive.
In conclusion, I wouldn’t jump at the opportunity
to turn Weeping Willow another time but if that
was all I had, I wouldn’t turn it down. I would definitely endeavour to incorporate any of the bud
clusters in the piece, so hollowforms come to
mind.
Tree of Heaven
Again, from an “Info@” email (as well as Facebook
Marketplace at the same time) we were notified of
a “Tree of Heaven” being available. It was very
large with about a 48” diameter, so my 24” bar was
just able to meet it in the middle. A few of us took
a fair load of it away.
Tree of Heaven is a ring-porous wood with all the
appearance of Ash, so quite “blonde” with very distinctive grain. Upon checking with Uncle Google, I
learned that it was very soft. “Softness” without a
reference to a hardness scale is a relative term. I
found it to be “not soft”. While not “really hard” it
didn’t seem “soft” at all. Certainly not nearly as soft
as the weeping willow. I cored it out into bowl
forms, so it remains to be seen how it is to work
when it’s dry. For now, I would put it in the category of working green Big Leaf Maple or Cherry.
I’m certain the wood will be attractive when it is
dry. I don’t know exactly what to expect while drying but I doubt it will have any unusual amount of
stress in it, so expect to re-turn it successfully. Being a ring-porous wood with quite open pores it
would be an outstanding choice for liming. From a
utilitarian standpoint, I probably wouldn’t use it for
a salad bowl, but it would make a great fruit bowl
or platter. It will certainly look nice on a table.
It seemed mildly abrasive while turning but a lot of
(Continued on page 10)

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
woods are like that when turned green. It cut
cleanly and made heaps of really great shavings. I
had a lot of fun turning this stuff.
I’m happy with this wood and can’t wait to turn it
to finish. I may be of a mind to do some liming at
the time. If I do, I don’t think I will colour the wood
and will probably use a clear finish with black in the
grain. Don’t get in my way if this stuff comes up
again.
(Continued from page 9)
Adventures for In Person Turning with Others By Sheila Balzer, WIT Liaison
Others have tried to explain that I have been missing out given that I began turning while restrictions
were in place so most of my turning experiences to
date have been remote, online, and watching others mixed in with a few moments of showing others how to turn. Joyfully, the transition to In Person turning has begun.
On October 14th, KMS was back to having some
turners come in a do live demos. There I got to
meet the two Dan’s (Dan Breck and Dan Moleschi)
who were messing around at the lathe and patiently showing their skills to curious on lookers. Dan
Moleschi was making gorgeous pens (oooohhh,
ahhhh) while Dan Breck showed me and others
various steps for making the cuts and measurements for turning a bowl. Yes, it was very helpful
to see it live!
Then on another outing, Diana and I made the trek
to Gary’s who has three lathes in his shop so we
could each have a go. Soooooo many things to try
to learn, and so little time. During this adventure I
got to see firsthand about riding the bevel which
helped me understand why and how I had to
change my approach to use my gouges since Larry
made adjustments to the angles. This was huge
for me.
(Continued on page 11)

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
We started our day by turning a top. While Gary
and Diana were super speedy, I took my sweet
time, enjoying the cuts and process, until I caught
at just the wrong angle, and it popped off (this is
why I like turning small stuff). Gary thought there
was no way I could get it back on for turning to get
it done. After some lunch, the challenge was accepted.
Then he mentioned that some tops can turn either
way…oh, I’ve got to do that. I took my sweet time,
played some more, and got my top to spin top and
bottom, despite it no longer being completely balanced and round.
During our time together we discovered that each
of us have very different approaches to turning,
and that’s swell. The world of woodturning would
be a very boring place if we all turned the same
thing in the same way. I so very much appreciate
the diversity I have seen and experienced since diving into this sliver of the creative world.
Also,
during
this visit, I salvaged a couple
of pieces from
Gary
Burns’
burn pile…sure,
this one was
cracked, but it
was
almost
there,
I
saw
some possibility for play and
creative experimentation.
The next time I
went to the lathe, I took it along and am making it
into a collaborative project. It still is a work-in-play
as there are more things I want to try before being
done. I very much appreciate having a chunk of
wood that I could do no worse to. For me, there is
a sense of freedom I find by being creative with
someone cast offs. I’m hoping it will give me more
confidence as I approach the treasured boxes of
wood from Barry’s personal wood stash.
Slowly I am reaching the conclusion that while it is
possible to see the tool control and gentle cuts
from a master like John Jordan online, there really
is something to being in the same place and space
working with others who share a passion and appreciation.
The biggest challenges these days and in the days
ahead are to find a chunk of time to play at the
lathe. But I’m pleased to accept this challenge given the welcoming home of our new puppy, Mando.
Oh gosh he is cute, full of energy, curiosity, growing and learning so very fast. To be that young
again, learning so quickly and growing every time
he sleeps. Also being open to a wide variety of
people, experiences, and approaches…so very
much like my early days of becoming a
woodturner.
(Continued from page 10)

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
Tell us about your background – how did
you get into wood turning?
My first introduction to wood turning occurred in
the late1950’s at Junior High School in Edmonton,
grades 7,8 and 9. I still have the first bowl I turned
using a face plate of laminated Tennessee Cedar. It
was five decades later in 2007 that I renewed my
interest and started to attend the GVWG meetings.
Tell us about your workshop/ studio.
My shop is located on the ground / garage level of
our Steveston home. The shop is 285 Sq feet. Every
bench, storage rack and cabinet are on wheels.
There are two work benches, a table saw, router
table, band saw, standing drill press, radial arm
saw, and an abundance of hand and power hand
tools. Tool cabinets are repurposed optical fixtures. A Craftsman tool cabinet, and a set of medical specimen drawers to hold bolts, nuts, screws
and miscellaneous bits and pieces. My lathe is a
Nova 1624 belt drive with extend bed, out-rigger
along with a vacuum system. Dust collection consists of a Delta 2 stage 50-660c, Ridgid Air Filtration
System AF3000 and Ridgid Job Site system near the
lathe. Lighting has been upgraded to LED 48”
tubes.
(Continued on page 13)
Guild Member Profile
- Robert (Bob) James
By Bob James
First bowl in high school
Shop entrance
Right side of shop

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
What tools do you most like using on your
lathe?
I do not have a favorite tool however when they
function as intended, with the chips flying or the
shavings curling, you know you are in the zone. I
have occasionally cursed a tool for what is has
done knowing full well that it was the person on
the handle that caused the design opportunity
through poor technique, dull edge or one last cut.
What is your favorite wood?
Walnut followed by west coast maple along with
cherry are the woods that I typically choose to
work with. Their various colours and patterns provide unique pieces.
What finishes do you prefer using?
Polymerized tung oil or a custom finish consisting
of melted beeswax, coconut oil and walnut oil as
they provide a low luster finish that I prefer.
Do you ever incorporate other materials
into your pieces?
I have included metal components, resin, along
with stains, paints, and burning to enhance my
work. A set of Caulking Mallets that included copper bands are some of my favorite pieces.
What other types of woodworking or pursuits do you have?
I have built several projects after moving into our
current residence including my office furniture,
[desk, bookshelves, drawer units and filing cabinets], and display shelving units in our great room.
In 2014-2015 over 6 months, I built “Y Knot”, a
Chesapeake Light Craft, Passagemaker [Take-Apart]
Dinghy. Length 11”4”, beam 56” Draft rowing 6”,
Sailing 30”.
(Continued from page 12)
(Continued on page 14)
Turning area
Left side of shop
Caulking Mallets

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 14
“Y Knot”
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
Inspiration comes to me from nature and media
used by other artists as well as pottery, native craft
art and of course other turners and woodworkers.
Who has been the greatest influence on
your work?
The demonstrators and instructor of the Greater
Vancouver Woodturning Guild have provided incite, direction, guidance, and motivation from the
first meeting I attended. The outside demonstrators and now the IRD’s have provided many nuggets and ideas on where one can take their
woodturning direction.
Where do you usually display and/or sell
your work?
My work is displayed in our home and as gifts for
family and friends. I have not attempted to sell my
work. The time in the shop provides me therapeutic and mental stress relief even as the noise and
dust may disrupt significant others.
What is the most challenging piece that
you have made so far?
The ”Jack” for the collaborative challenge several
years ago was a trying piece at the time. It required many attempts to turn the components to a
uniform presentation.
Where do you see your work going in the
future?
A recent article in the AAW Publication showing
“Miniature Turnings” has peaked my interest as it
would use up the small scrapes that are about the
shop.
Are there any new techniques you would
like to try?
Beadwork and texturing are some of the techniques that may appear in my future endeavors.
Where do you think you most need to improve?
Practice, practice, practice as repetition improves
the muscle memory. Seek out and attempt new
techniques, procedures to improve my skill level.
As a member of the GVWG, I have assisted in the
setup, tear down of the in-person guild meetings,
the 2007 and 2010 symposiums, AV presentations
at guild meetings. I would like to update my
knowledge as it relates to IRD procedures, equipment, and presentations in assisting the guild and
its membership.
(Continued from page 13)

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 15
Ordering Custom
-Made Turning Smocks 2022
By David Sweet O.C.
Our Guild members are invited to order made-tomeasure turning smocks from the professional
seamstress that also designed and sewed smocks
for many of us in mid-2019. Several members have
expressed an interest in buying an additional
smock while others missed the first opportunity
and have requested that we arrange for a second
order. The value and fit (made to your measurements!) of these smocks is exceptional. They are
priced at $90, all in. We can also purchase our own
fabric plus sewing notions and have the smock
sewn to your specifications for $50. The smocks
will be made for us in January 2022.
Since the Guild is not meeting in person at the moment, the orders will be submitted to the seamstress via email. And the payments (in advance)
will be made via e-transfer to the seamstress’s
email address. You are encouraged to place your
orders now and to make your e-payments so that
the smocks can be made in January. Details are
included in the order form that appears in this edition of the newsletter. I will pick up the orders
when they are complete and then bring your
smock to the in-person meetings when we meet
again at the Sapperton Hall (fingers crossed!).
The smocks are available in your choice of two fabrics. The first fabric is a cotton-polyester blend that
comes in a beige colour. This fabric is medium
weight, it is cozy on cold winter days. The second
fabric is a rip-stop nylon material that comes in a
charcoal colour with a light gray square pattern on
it. It is light weight, easily sheds shavings, and is
cool on summer days. If you wish to supply your
own fabric in your favourite colour (see Photos 3A
and 3B) you must also submit a matching front zipper (20-22” long), Velcro for the arm and neck closures (20 cm long), and thread. The amount of fabric needed if you supply your own is 2.75 square
meters from a 54” or 60” wide bolt.
There are several choices for pockets, for example
at the lower back on each side; small, vertical pock-
(Continued on page 16)
Beige Cotton-Polyester Blend
Charcoal Rip-Stop Nylon

November 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 16
ets for pencils and rulers, etc. at the top of each
sleeve; and a pocket with a flap on the chest. You
can specify if you want none, one or all of these
pockets on your smock. You also have options for
vents to be added across the upper back and also
under the arms. Many of the 2019 smocks included vents and most turners with vents would not be
without them. The Guild logo will be embroidered
on to the chest and you have an option of having
your name embroidered on the other side of the
chest too.
You also have a choice of sleeve lengths. In general, the options include: short sleeves (above the
elbows), 3/4 sleeves (just below the elbows), and
long sleeves (to the wrists). Each option includes
Velcro at the end of the sleeve to adjust the fit to
keep shavings out of the sleeves. This is also present at the neck for the same reason. Please specify the length of sleeve (in inches) that you choose
in the designated place on the order form.
To complete your order, take five measurements
as shown in the diagram on the order form, and
then submit these with your name, phone number
and email address to the seamstress: Emmerentia
Schutte at the email address on the form. Then etransfer your payment to the same email address.
I received a lot of help with this project from the
following Guild members: Barry Wilkinson, Cathy
Friesen, Rick Stuible, and Dex Hallwood. Thank you
very much!
(Continued from page 15)
Custom Fabric Colour
"Fire Wand" - controls fire, but can neither
start nor extinguish it.
I had never made a magic wand. However I did
know one thing about them and that is the simpler
the wand, the more power they can channel. For
that reason the magic delivery tip is plain. The middle section is an insulator between fire and magician. The twisted end is awkward to handle and
renders the wand powerless unless properly
gripped.
Turned from Arbutus. Charged with fire. Unfinished
(otherwise it's just a baton).

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
